Accepting the cookie makes CSRF the next question, and the query-string uuid read is the sharp edge. api.py:210 falls back to `request.args.get("uuid")`, so the endpoint is triggerable by a cross-site HTML form POST with no JSON and no custom header — the one shape that carries cookies. `VIEW_COOKIE` is `samesite="Lax"`, and Lax withholds cookies on cross-site POST, so this is closed today; but it is closed by one keyword in an unrelated function. Separately, `@cross_origin()` currently echoes any Origin (verified live), so tighten it on this route regardless.

(ii) 441 MB is not an OOM on a 512 MB dyno — Heroku R14 fires above quota and R15/SIGKILL far above; 441 MB is 86% of quota. (iii) I could not reproduce 441 MB and it is not derivable from my numbers by the claim's own linear-in-days model (0.543 MB/day x 183 = 99 MB payload, and the merge-driven estimate is ~76 MB -> ~374 MiB peak in a bare process). My process was at 139.7 MiB peak already holding the 30.43 MB body, i.e. ~109 MiB of interpreter + imports baseline; the increment attributable to fetch+parse is ~**106 MiB**, and on the worker dyno it sits on top of a larger baseline, so the true peak would exceed 215 MB.

6. The clamp is not the big lever it reads as. Exact counts: release 56d = 20,094 changesets vs release 30d = **13,041** — the clamp removes only 35% of the payload today (30.43 MB -> ~19.7 MB). It does cut `Changeset.add` 276.1 s -> **121.8 s (-56%)** because the per-node cost is superlinear (3.85 ms/node at 2,000; 13.74 at 20,094), and its real value is bounding growth forever. It is not a fix for the 335 s.
